name: Horizontal stripes and layering for width

lead: People wear horizontal stripes and stacked layers to make the chest and shoulders look wider and the upper body bulkier, with the effect visible as soon as the outfit is on.

Layers add real fabric volume around the torso, and horizontal patterns are said to lead the eye sideways across the body. No direct studies of stripes or layering on perceived body width were found; related illusion research uses line drawings, not clothing.

paras: People choose horizontally striped tops, thicker knits, and layered shirts, tees and jackets, often on slimmer frames wanting more upper-body presence. The effect is immediate and works with any wardrobe.
No health risks apply. Heavy layering can add bulk at the waist as well as the chest, and in hot weather it can be uncomfortable.

angle.text: People wear horizontal stripes and layers to look broader across the chest and shoulders; layers add real volume and stripes are said to draw the eye sideways. The effect is immediate with clothing alone. No direct studies were found.

lead: Horizontal stripes and layering are two clothing techniques people use to change how the upper body reads in clothes. Layering, such as a jacket over a sweater over a shirt, adds real fabric thickness around the shoulders, chest and arms, so a slim frame takes up more visual space. Horizontal stripes are used on the belief that lines running across the torso lead the eye sideways and make the chest and shoulders look broader.

The stripe idea is old and widely held. A 2022 study traced a version of it to an 1813 Japanese beauty handbook, and a 2026 study found the popular belief that horizontal stripes widen the body common among participants in Greece and the Netherlands [1][2]. It is also one of the most studied questions in clothing perception, because it runs against the Helmholtz illusion: a square filled with horizontal lines tends to be judged taller and narrower than the same square filled with vertical lines [3].

Laboratory studies since 2011 have asked how striped garments change perceived body size. Thompson and Mikellidou reported that horizontal stripes did not make figures look fatter, and later work found that horizontally striped and darker dresses looked thinner than plain ones, though effects vary with the figure, the stripe spacing and the viewer [3][4][2][2]. Layering has not been the subject of a comparable perception study; its effect is the physical bulk of the added garments.

paras: Practitioners describe two separate ideas. One is that stripe orientation changes the apparent shape of the torso. The other is that layering adds bulk where the wearer is slim. Common layered combinations include jackets over knitwear over shirts, overshirts, and thicker fabrics at the shoulder and chest.

The two techniques act by different routes. Layering alters the actual outline of the clothed body, so its effect does not depend on a perceptual illusion. Stripes alter only the pattern on the surface, and their effect depends on how viewers perceive pattern, colour and shape.

The Helmholtz illusion is the effect in which a square filled with horizontal lines is judged to be taller and narrower than an otherwise identical square filled with vertical lines [3]. In Thompson and Mikellidou's 2011 paper in i-Perception, a vertically striped rectangle had to be extended about 7.1 percent vertically to match the perceived height of a horizontally striped square, and a horizontally striped rectangle had to be about 4.5 percent wider to match the perceived width of a vertically striped square [3]. The effect was reported for a line drawing of a woman and for stereoscopically viewed photographs of a half-body mannequin, while an experiment with a three-dimensional cylinder found no evidence that horizontal lines look fattening; the authors concluded that their results supported Helmholtz's original claim [3].

In 2013 Ashida, Kuraguchi and Miyoshi reported that horizontally striped figures looked thinner, but that the effect was stronger for thin figures than for heavier ones and might reverse for the latter [4]. They also found wide variation between participants, possibly depending on which features viewers attended to, and a strong effect of the order in which thin and heavier figures were shown [4]. They concluded that even this simple geometric illusion is complex in everyday perception [4].

Koutsoumpis, Economou and van der Burg (Perception, 2021) tested photographs of a real model rather than geometric shapes. They compared horizontal stripes against no stripes and controlled the dress's average luminance. Horizontal stripes and lower luminance each had a small-to-moderate thinning effect on perceived body size, the effects were larger together, and the luminance effect was stronger against a darker background [2].

A 2026 PLoS One paper by Koutsoumpis and colleagues compared beliefs with perception in 316 participants in Greece and the Netherlands and 419 in Greece, the Netherlands and Taiwan. A striped dress was perceived as thinner than a plain one, the stronger a person believed stripes make people look thinner the more they judged the striped dress thinner, and belief that stripes widen did not significantly predict their judgments; no cross-country differences emerged [2].

Chen and Peng (i-Perception, 2026) responded to critics who said earlier work lacked ecological validity and tested only pencil-stripe patterns. In a survey of 214 participants using five stripe-spacing types, a horizontally pencil-striped dress was rated slimmest, while equidistant stripes made the body look slimmer when vertical, reversing the pencil-stripe pattern; men and women differed slightly [2].

Layering adds fabric at the shoulders, chest and upper arms, and wearers use structured outer layers, overshirts and knitwear to increase the apparent size of a slim torso. No perception study found tests layered outfits against single garments for apparent body width, so claims about layering rest on the physical effect of added thickness and on wearers' reports. Wikipedia's page on the term describes layering mainly as wearing several lightweight garments for warmth [5].

The vertical-horizontal illusion, in which a vertical line is overestimated in length relative to an equal horizontal line, persists even when observers know the lines match, and is a separate effect from the Helmholtz illusion [6]. Wikipedia's account notes that the illusion is largest in L, plus and inverted-T figures and that susceptibility varies with age and between urban and rural populations [6].

Miyazaki and Ishibashi found the belief that horizontal stripes make a person look wider and shorter, and vertical stripes slimmer and taller, in Miyako Fuzoku Kewai Den, an 1813 Japanese book on beauty and customs in Edo, written when vertical striped clothing was becoming popular [1]. They concluded that the belief was established more than two centuries ago, even though it conflicts with the Helmholtz illusion [1].
No studies found. Laboratory perception studies of striped shapes, figures and dresses are described above [3][4][2][2][2].

lore.intro: Advice about stripes and layers circulates in style and fitness circles as general wisdom about making a slim frame look bigger. Research on the belief shows it is common across several countries and has a long history [1][2].

claims.claim: Horizontal stripes make the torso look wider.
Layering adds bulk and makes a slim person look bigger.
Dark colours make you look slimmer, so lighter colours add size.
Stripe width and spacing do not matter.
Belief in the stripe effect shapes what people see.
The stripe effect is the same for all body shapes.

timeline.event: A Japanese beauty handbook records the belief that striped clothing alters perceived body shape. [1]
Thompson and Mikellidou publish tests of the Helmholtz illusion applied to fashion. [3]
Ashida and colleagues report that the Helmholtz effect varies with figure shape and viewer. [4]
Koutsoumpis and colleagues find horizontal stripes and darker dresses thin a photographed model. [2]
Miyazaki and Ishibashi trace the stripe belief to the 1813 handbook. [1]
Koutsoumpis et al. report the stripe belief across three countries; Chen and Peng compare stripe spacings. [2][2]
